I think you're correct on most if not all points. I think the ultimate goal though is to expose kids at a young age to coding to see if they'll like it or not enough to pursue it. Some kids may be natural coders and not even know it because they were never properly introduced to it. I work in an online school setting and we did the Hour of Code this year and one middle school girl got hooked and could't stop talking about coding and researching coding and asking questions about coding. She was definitely in the minority but I'm glad we did the HoC as she may never have known she was even interested in things like that.

One thing I will say is that most of the people behind this movement are probably in my age bracket where we grew up with computers being The New Cool Thing. Back in the 70's and 80's, computers were more of a tool and less of an appliance. When you unboxed them on Christmas Morning, they didn't do anything except blink stupidly at you. You had to learn how to use them. Today, things are very different. You unbox them, set up your account and within minutes are going about doing things. So most middle or high school kids as a rule today don't have the need or desire to make the computer do anything new or different because nearly everything they want is already there. But get them when they're young enough with simple little things like Scratch on a Raspberry Pi, and suddenly those little minds start to think up The Next Big Thing. And that's what we need again. Our schools, at least here in the U.S., seemed to give up on teaching coding in the early to mid 90's in favor of lessons in MS Word and PowerPoint. Not a bad thing in and of itself as the kids use these programs all the time, but if that's the limit of a student's 'computer class', than it's a shame. Not everyone will be a coder, but everyone should have the chance to figure out if they are or not.

I was actually born in the 90s and currently studying computer engineering because I had a fascination with computers. This wasn't because I was told "Hey coding is cool" but rather I had a computer at home when I was in elementary school and I wanted to figure out how this appliance worked from the inside out, just like playing with LEGOs or other toys where you put together and take apart (IKEA furniture is fun for me).

As for middle and high school students, I'm pretty sure it hasn't changed for a long time, but most of the students just want to look cool in front of their friends. The notion of "Smart = Sexy" hasn't really sunk in yet for 90% of the students. The reason why they don't have a desire to make the computer do anything new is because they simply don't care, which is why the underlying structure of learning and teaching needs to change.

How do we teach children to be passionate about learning and spending their own time to make something on their own. Coding is a huge resource for them to make something, but if the children are nonchalant about it then it's effectively wasted. This is why I believe that schools should be separated into skill levels over seniority, because this gives incentive for students to go learn. If you're going to graduate after x number of years, there's no real reason why you should study or learn. Those who are passionate about learning and creating will inherently be drawn to coding because of its potential, and even if they choose not to be a coder it is an attitude that they will carry on into whatever profession they choose.
